title: Interim Evaluation of the Horizon Europe Framework Programme (2021-2024), Annex 16: Evaluation of EuroHPC JU (SWD(2025) 110, Part 8/21)
venue: Commission Staff Working Document SWD(2025) 110 final, Part 8/21 (Council doc. 8526/25 ADD 8)
method: interim evaluation drawing on external support study, programme monitoring data, TOP500 statistics and stakeholder input; descriptive
outcomes: EU supercomputing capacity and global share, R&I outputs, leverage of private funding, openness to users
headline: Since EuroHPC, the EU's share of global TOP500 supercomputing capacity rose from 12% to 20.8%, with three EuroHPC systems in the world top 10, though the evaluation says it is still too early to assess the impact of funded R&I projects and the private leverage factor is low.
summary_plain: The Commission's review of the EU supercomputing partnership finds that Europe now has a much bigger share of the world's top supercomputers than before. It says most research projects are still running, so their effects cannot yet be judged.
quality: Descriptive self-evaluation with no counterfactual; attribution of capacity growth to the JU is asserted rather than tested; separate from the Digital Europe interim evaluation already listed.
interested_party: European Commission evaluating its own partnership

title: EuroHPC JU Consolidated Annual Activity Report 2025
method: annual monitoring report with KPI table and access-call statistics; descriptive
outcomes: compute resources awarded, proposals and approval rates, operational supercomputers and quantum computers, KPI status
headline: In 2025 EuroHPC ran 53 access cut-offs, received 1,603 proposals and awarded 1,301 (81% approval), allocating 54,998,115 node hours across its systems; it reports all JU-specific KPIs (e.g. operational supercomputers, projects accessing systems) as on target.
summary_plain: The EU supercomputing body's own yearly report counts how much computing time it gave out in 2025 and to how many projects. It says it is meeting all of its own targets.
quality: Self-reported output data, no outcome or counterfactual analysis; useful as activity monitoring under Regulation 2021/1173.
interested_party: Reporting body is the Joint Undertaking itself

authors: European Innovation Council and SMEs Executive Agency (EISMEA) / Enterprise Europe Network
title: Enterprise Europe Network Impact Report 2022-2025
venue: EISMEA / Enterprise Europe Network (reported by EEN Czechia)
method: self-reported outcome rates from EEN client impact surveys; descriptive, no comparison group
outcomes: SME innovation, internationalisation, funding obtained, digital adoption, sustainability measures among EEN clients
headline: Among SMEs supported by the SMP-funded Enterprise Europe Network in 2022-2025, 90% introduced new or improved products or processes, 84% entered new markets (79% in other EU countries), 78% obtained funding, 88% adopted digital solutions and 91% took steps to cut environmental impact.
summary_plain: The EU business support network paid for by the Single Market Programme says most of the small firms it helped went on to innovate, export or get funding. These figures come from the firms' own answers, with no comparison to firms that got no help.
quality: Client self-reports, selection bias likely, no counterfactual; full PDF could not be opened (blocked), figures taken from official EEN national partner page.
interested_party: Published by the agency that runs the network (EU executive agency)

title: The Economic Review of Industrial Design in Europe - Final Report (MARKT/2013/064//D2/ST/OP)
venue: Study for the European Commission, DG Internal Market and Services
method: Eurostat sector data analysis, WIPO filing data, firm-level database, online survey of design-intensive firms (about 80-140 valid responses per question) and structured interviews
outcomes: economic contribution of design-intensive industries, use of registered vs informal design protection, effects of non-harmonised spare-parts protection
headline: Under the predecessor Design Directive 98/71, 3.4m firms in design-intensive industries employing 23m people added about EUR 1.7trn to EU value added, but only a minority of designs are formally protected; the study finds no good economic or IP justification for design protection of visible spare parts and recommends an EU-wide repair clause.
summary_plain: This study looked at how firms used EU design rights under the old directive that the 2024 Directive replaces. It found most designs are never registered, and it recommended letting independent makers sell visible car spare parts, which the 2024 Directive now does.
quality: Predecessor-regime evidence (Directive 98/71/EC, recast by 2024/2823); descriptive plus small non-random survey; not causal.

authors: Katharina Gangl, Michael K. Zuern, Tobias Biro
title: The "Right to Repair" Under Scrutiny: A Study on Repair Culture in Germany in Light of New Political Framework Conditions (NIMpulse 20)
venue: Nuremberg Institute for Market Decisions (NIM), June 2026
method: repeated population-representative online survey in Germany (n=2,000 in 2025; n=3,500 in April-May 2026) plus choice experiment (n=500)
outcomes: repair rates, repair spending, willingness to pay for repair, knowledge of the Directive, attitude shifts
headline: Just before the Directive applied, only about one in three broken electronic devices in German households was repaired; willingness to pay for repair barely changed between 2025 and 2026, and while 80% knew about the new information duty, 63% wrongly believed retailers will have to carry out repairs and 18% thought repairs would be free.
summary_plain: A large German survey taken just before the EU repair rules started found people still repair only about a third of broken gadgets, and many misunderstand what the new law requires. The authors expect the law alone will not change repair habits much.
quality: Large repeated survey giving a pre-application baseline; self-reported behaviour; no counterfactual; one country.
interested_party: Institute founded by GfK; states it is self-funded

title: Study supporting the implementation of interoperability assessments in EU public administrations - Final report
method: 11-month implementation study: interviews, co-creation workshops, surveys and validation sessions with 132 stakeholders from nearly all Member States, plus 8 case studies
outcomes: readiness and barriers for mandatory interoperability assessments under the Act
headline: Consulting 132 stakeholders across nearly all Member States in the Act's first year, the study concludes the basic elements needed to start mandatory interoperability assessments are already in place, and makes 34 recommendations on tools, skills and governance.
summary_plain: A study for the Commission asked public administrations how ready they are to carry out the new interoperability checks the Act requires. It found the basics are in place but more tools, training and coordination are needed.
quality: Qualitative implementation study, landing page only read; contractor not named on the page; no quantitative outcome data.

authors: Ilsa Godlovitch, Peter Kroon, Sonia Strube Martins, Saskja Schaefer, Stefano Lucidi, Nico Steffen, Thomas Plueckebaum, Cara Schwarz-Schilling (WIK-Consult); Facundo Herrera, Ricardas Juskevicius (ICF)
title: Support Study associated with the Review of the Broadband Cost Reduction Directive: Evaluation Report
venue: Study for the European Commission, DG CNECT (Publications Office, doi:10.2759/560564)
method: ex-post evaluation of the predecessor Directive 2014/61/EU: stakeholder survey, 56 structured interviews, case studies in 12 Member States, desk research
outcomes: network roll-out enabled, cost savings from infrastructure access, use of permit and transparency measures
headline: Where effectively applied, the Broadband Cost Reduction Directive (replaced by the GIA) contributed at least 100,000 km of additional network roll-out in 2016-2020, and operators benefiting from access to physical infrastructure reported 10-30% cost savings, though application varied widely across provisions and countries.
summary_plain: Before the Gigabit Infrastructure Act replaced it, the earlier EU law on cheaper broadband roll-out was evaluated. It helped build extra network where countries applied it properly, but results were uneven, which shaped the new Act.
quality: Predecessor-provision evaluation (GIA repeals and extends Directive 2014/61/EU); survey and case evidence, no counterfactual; figures partly from interested operators.
interested_party: Commissioned by the European Commission; cost-saving figures self-reported by telecom operators

authors: Zoi Kolitsi (AUTH), Mathias Maurer (Austrian Federal Ministry of Justice) and SimpliVi partners
title: SimpliVi Analysis & Design Consolidation (v1.1)
method: qualitative field study: study visits, interviews and questionnaires with judges, court staff, ministries, lawyers and IT staff in 14 EU Member States plus Brazil, Canada and Norway (2023-2025)
outcomes: use of videoconferencing in court hearings, barriers to cross-border videoconferencing, reported efficiency effects
headline: Field research in 14 Member States finds rules on remote hearings still differ widely, and that cross-border videoconferencing is held back by missing contact points, incompatible proprietary systems and legal differences; reported benefits include fewer prisoner transports and faster case closure.
summary_plain: An EU-funded project visited courts across Europe to see how video hearings work, as the new EU digital justice rules start to require them. It found big differences between countries and technical and legal hurdles for hearings across borders.
period_geography: 2023-2025; 14 EU Member States plus Brazil, Canada, Norway
quality: Qualitative baseline mostly before the Regulation's videoconference provisions apply; no quantified outcomes; consortium includes justice ministries.
interested_party: Consortium includes national justice ministries; EU-funded

authors: CERT-EU (Cybersecurity Service for the Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies)
title: Threat Landscape Report 2025: A Year in Review
method: annual threat and incident monitoring under Regulation 2023/2841, including counts of significant incidents reported under Article 21; descriptive
outcomes: significant incidents at Union entities, threat actors, initial access vectors, critical exposures
headline: Significant incidents at EU institutions, bodies and agencies fell from 15 in 2024 to nine in 2025 (seven via vulnerability exploitation), and critical exposures to threat actors fell from 20 to 5, while tracked threat actors rose from 110 to 174; CERT-EU says the cause of the drop is unclear.
summary_plain: The EU's own cyber-response team counts serious cyber incidents hitting EU institutions under the new rules. Serious incidents fell in 2025 compared with 2024, even though more hacker groups were targeting the institutions.
period_geography: 2024-2025; EU institutions, bodies, offices and agencies
quality: Official incident counts from the Regulation's reporting duty; two years only, small numbers, no attribution of the change to the Regulation.
interested_party: CERT-EU is a body set up under the Regulation

title: KPMG EU Digital Product Passport Readiness Survey
method: survey of 70+ organisations across Europe (44% textiles, 16% metals, 12% batteries, 10% electronics, 10% furniture)
outcomes: awareness, understanding and readiness for ESPR Digital Product Passport obligations
headline: 97% of surveyed firms had heard of the Digital Product Passport but only 33% reported high understanding of the requirements; 53% were just 'getting started', 19% 'well-prepared', 16% 'starting soon' and 12% unprepared, and 23% had not assigned responsibility.
summary_plain: A consultancy survey of about 70 European companies found nearly all know about the new digital product passport, but only about one in five feel well prepared for it.
quality: Small non-random sample from a consultancy selling DPP services; readiness self-assessed; no counterfactual.

searched: searched: ECA special reports on EES/ETIAS/interoperability, FRA reports, Statewatch, eu-LISA EES statistics (EES is under Reg. 2017/2226, not 2019/817), Commission state-of-play reports (COM(2026) 446 is the sixth report already listed); found no new ex-post study of the interoperability components (ESP, sBMS, CIR, MID)
